t.socotra archipelago@12.5,53.8:
Let us be honest from the first line: you will not ride your own motorcycle here, and you should think carefully before going at all. Socotra is an island in the Arabian Sea, part of Yemen, about three hundred and fifty kilometres off the coast of the Arabian Peninsula and closer to the Horn of Africa. Isolated for millions of years, it developed a flora and fauna found nowhere else on earth, and roughly a third of its plants are endemic. The most famous is the dragon's blood tree, shaped like an inverted umbrella, whose red resin has been traded since ancient times as a dye and medicine. The archipelago was listed by UNESCO in 2008 for its extraordinary biodiversity.

The landscapes are otherworldly: limestone plateaus covered with dragon's blood trees, bottle trees with swollen trunks and pink flowers, white sand dunes running down to turquoise water, granite mountains, caves and lagoons. Hadibu, about twenty-six kilometres from this point, is the main town, a modest place where most visitors stay before heading out with a local guide and driver.

The island's people speak Soqotri, an ancient language related to the languages of southern Arabia, and they have a rich tradition of poetry. Their way of life, based on herding, fishing and date cultivation, is adapted to the harsh climate, with strong monsoon winds from June to September that make the sea rough and limit access. The best time to visit is from October to April.

Yemen has been at war for years, and while Socotra has been relatively calm, the political situation is complex and governments generally advise against travel to Yemen. Access is limited to occasional flights, and visiting usually requires organising a tour through an approved operator, who will arrange permits, transport and accommodation. Vehicles are rented with drivers, and the roads, some paved, many rough tracks, are best left to local experts. Fuel is available in Hadibu, but supplies can be unreliable. If you do go, respect local customs, dress modestly and leave nothing behind but footprints, as the island's ecosystem is fragile and unique.
t.anjireh ajori@32.2,54.5:
Thirty kilometres from Yazd, out on the gravel plains where the Shirkuh mountains rise to the south-west and the Dasht-e Kavir stretches away towards the north, the ground is threaded with lines of small craters. Each crater is the mouth of a shaft dropping down to a qanat, an underground channel that carries water by gravity from the foot of the mountains to villages and fields many kilometres away. The Persian qanat is one of the great engineering achievements of the ancient world, and a selection of these systems is listed by UNESCO. Anjireh Ājori sits in this landscape, one of the places where the old desert infrastructure of water, shelter and trade can still be traced.

To understand the region, start in Yazd. The old city, a World Heritage site, is built almost entirely of mud brick, a maze of narrow lanes, domed roofs and tall windcatchers, the badgirs that channel breezes down into houses to cool them. Yazd is also a centre of the Zoroastrian faith; a fire is said to have burned in its fire temple for centuries, and on a hill outside the city stand the Towers of Silence, where the dead were once laid out for the birds. In the desert around, old caravanserais mark the trade routes, including the round, fortress-like Zein-o-din caravanserai to the south-east, now restored as a place to stay.

Riding in Iran is a serious undertaking and needs honest preparation. Check your government's travel advice, visa rules and the regulations for bringing a foreign motorcycle, which usually means a carnet de passages. Conditions can change quickly, and some nationalities face particular restrictions.

The roads around Yazd are mostly wide and straight, crossing open desert with mountains on the horizon. Traffic can be fast and unpredictable, with trucks and cars overtaking in unexpected places. The heat in summer is extreme, often above forty degrees, while winter nights can be freezing. Sandstorms can reduce visibility suddenly. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, ideally riding early and resting in the middle of the day.

Yazd, with nearly half a million people, is the place for fuel, food and repairs. Stations in the open desert are few, so fill up before heading out. Try a cool glass of faloodeh, a frozen sweet, or Yazdi cakes and pastries, and drink plenty of water.

The dragon's blood tree looks like an umbrella turned inside out, with a dense crown of branches spreading from a thick trunk, and it grows almost nowhere else on earth but the island of Socotra, in the Arabian Sea between Yemen and Somalia. Its red resin was traded in antiquity as a dye and medicine. Socotra has been isolated for millions of years, and about a third of its plant species are found nowhere else, including bottle trees with swollen trunks, desert roses and frankincense trees. UNESCO lists the archipelago for its extraordinary biodiversity.

Hadibu is the main town, on the northern coast, a dusty place of a few thousand people with a small harbour and a market. Behind it rise the granite peaks of the Hajhir mountains, and the plateaus of Homhil and Dixam, where the dragon's blood trees grow in forests, offer some of the strangest landscapes anywhere. The coast has white sand beaches, dunes and lagoons, and the sea is rich in fish and coral. The islanders speak Soqotri, a language related to ancient South Arabian tongues.

Riding here, honestly, is not something you can plan the usual way. Access to Socotra is limited to occasional flights and boats, and the island is affected by the wider conflict in Yemen, with political control shifting in recent years. Visitors typically come on organised tours with local guides and drivers, and bringing your own motorcycle is not realistic. Monsoon winds blow hard from June to September, when access is particularly difficult.

In Hadibu, there are small shops, simple restaurants and a few guesthouses, and fuel is available, but supplies can be irregular. Food is simple: rice, fish, goat and dates, with sweet tea. Before even thinking of travelling, check official advice carefully, as the situation can change fast. If you do get there, stand among the dragon's blood trees on the Dixam plateau at sunset, with the wind blowing and the strange shapes silhouetted against the sky; it feels like another planet.
t.samha@12.2,53.0:
Samha is a small, barren island in the Indian Ocean, one of the two islands known as the Brothers that lie between the main island of Socotra and the Horn of Africa. Together with Socotra and the other islands of the archipelago, it belongs to Yemen and is part of the Socotra Archipelago World Heritage Site, inscribed in 2008 for its extraordinary biodiversity. A few hundred people live on Samha, mostly fishermen, in a village by the shore, and the island has its own endemic plants, adapted to the harsh, dry climate.

Let me be honest: this is not a place for a motorcycle. Yemen has been at war for years, and while Socotra has been relatively calm, the situation is complex and travel requires careful planning, local contacts and up-to-date advice. If you go, you go as a traveller on foot, with a local guide and boat.

The reward for those who make it is a world unlike any other. Socotra is famous for its dragon's blood trees, with their umbrella-shaped crowns and red resin, and its bottle trees, frankincense trees and many other endemic plants. Samha shares some of this flora, and its coastal waters are full of fish, dolphins and coral. The cliffs and beaches are wild and empty, and the light is intense, with turquoise water against white sand and dark rock.

The people of the archipelago speak Soqotri, an ancient language related to the languages of southern Arabia, and their traditions of fishing, herding and poetry have developed in isolation for centuries. Life on Samha is simple and tough, with limited fresh water and few supplies from outside.

For riders, Samha is perhaps more of a dream than a destination, a reminder that some places remain beyond the reach of wheels. If the archipelago ever becomes more accessible, the main island of Socotra has a few roads that could offer an unusual ride, but for now, the best way to experience it is on foot, with patience, respect and a sense of adventure.
t.meidan emam@32.7,51.7:
Isfahan's great square is so large that the first time you walk into it from the bazaar side, your sense of scale goes briefly wrong. Meidan Emam, still widely known by its older name Naqsh-e Jahan, the image of the world, was laid out by Shah Abbas I when he made Isfahan the Safavid capital at the end of the sixteenth century. It is a long rectangle of two-storey arcades, a garden and fountains in the middle, and four buildings set into its sides that between them sum up an empire.

On the south end stands the Shah Mosque, now the Imam Mosque, its blue tilework so dense it seems to vibrate in the afternoon sun. On the east side sits the smaller Sheikh Lotfollah Mosque, which has no minarets and a dome that shifts from cream to pink as the light moves. Facing it is the Ali Qapu palace, with a raised veranda where the shah watched polo matches played on the square itself; the stone goalposts are still there at each end. To the north, the Qeysarieh gateway leads into the covered bazaar, which runs on for kilometres of copper beaters, carpet dealers, spice sellers and tea houses.

The riding itself is city riding, nothing more romantic than that. Isfahan traffic is dense and inventive, motorcycles swarm in every gap, and you will want to park well outside the square, which is pedestrian, and walk in. The rewards are evening ones. As the heat goes out of the day, families spread blankets on the lawns, horse carriages loop around the fountains, and the arcades fill with people who have come to do nothing in particular for a few hours. Get there for the last hour of light and stay after dark when the domes are lit.

Food is part of the stop. Try the local beryani, which in Isfahan means minced lamb cooked flat and served in bread rather than the rice dish of the same name elsewhere, and take a box of gaz, the pistachio nougat the city is famous for, for later in the saddle. Water and tea are easy to find, and fuel is plentiful in the city.

If you have time, ride a few minutes south to the Zayandeh Rud and the old Safavid bridges, Si-o-Se Pol and Khaju, where people gather under the arches in the evening. The river is often dry these days, which says something about water in central Iran, but the bridges are worth seeing either way.

Before planning any trip, check current travel advice and the rules for bringing a foreign motorcycle into the country, which involve paperwork and can change.

t.gabr abad@33.8,51.5:
Gabr Ābād lies out on the edge of the central Iranian desert, southeast of Kashan, in the kind of landscape where the road is a thin dark line and the horizon does most of the talking. The word gabr is an old Persian name for Zoroastrians, and it hints at how deep the layers here run. Long before Islam, this was country of fire temples and desert caravans, and Kashan itself has been a stop on trade routes between the plateau and the south for thousands of years.

Do not expect services at the site. It is a small settlement and a historical stop, not a town, so fill the tank in Kashan before you go and carry water, because the nearest reliable help can be a long way off. A small, light bike with a good range is the sensible tool, and heat is the real enemy. In July and August midday temperatures here can be brutal, so start at dawn or travel in spring and autumn, when the air is dry and clear and the desert shows its colours, ochre, pale grey and rust against distant blue mountains.

The riding is the plain kind: long straight asphalt, a few gentle bends where the road finds a dry watercourse, and wind that can lean on you from the side without warning. Trucks use the main roads, so keep to a calm pace and watch the shoulder for sand drift. Side tracks look inviting, but loose sand and soft clay on a loaded road bike is a bad combination, and a breakdown out here is a long, hot wait.

What makes the stop worth it is context. Kashan, a short ride to the northwest, is famous for its Persian gardens, traditional houses with wind-catcher towers and rosewater that scents the whole region in spring. The Karkas mountains rise to the southwest, with Natanz and the mountain village of Abyaneh beyond them, and a loop through that country makes sense of why the desert edge was settled at all. Ask locals for tea before you leave, and take what they say about road conditions seriously.
t.bagh e fin@33.9,51.4:
Bagh-e Fin is the garden people mean when they talk about Persian paradise gardens, and it sits at the southwestern edge of Kashan, right where the desert gives up and the mountains begin. The reason it exists is a spring. Water rises at the foot of the hills and has done for thousands of years, and the Safavid shah Abbas I turned it into a walled garden around the end of the sixteenth century, with straight channels, tall cypresses, fountains and a pavilion at the top of the slope, all organised around the idea that water in a dry land is a luxury worth building a palace for.

The gardeners did something clever. The spring feeds the pools by gravity alone, no pumps, so the fountains run because the ground tilts. On a hot afternoon the sound of it alone drops the temperature a couple of degrees. The garden is part of the UNESCO group of Persian Gardens, listed in 2011.

It also has a darker footnote. In 1852 Amir Kabir, the reforming chief minister who had tried to modernise Iran under the young Naser al-Din Shah, was murdered in the bathhouse here on royal orders. Visitors are shown the room, and the story gives the cool tiled halls an odd weight for a place so pretty.

Practically, Kashan is a city of several hundred thousand people, so fuel, food and hotels are easy, and you will not be stuck. The ride here from the desert side is long and flat, with the road entering town through an unremarkable ring of workshops before the old quarter opens up. Park near the garden entrance and go in early or late, because midday sun on bare paths is fierce and tour buses arrive in waves in spring.

Leave time for the old houses in the centre, built by rich carpet and rosewater merchants, with deep courtyards and wind-towers, and for a tea in a courtyard cafe. October and April are the best months, when the garden is green, the air is mild and snow is still on the far mountains.
t.maranjab@34.3,51.8:
Maranjāb is the place where the Kashan plain stops pretending to be gentle. A couple of hours' drive north-east of Kashan, past the oasis towns of Aran and Bidgol, the road gives out onto the Kavir, the great salt desert of central Iran, and a Safavid caravanserai sits there like a ship run aground in the sand. It was built to shelter trade caravans on a harsh route, with thick walls, a central courtyard and rooms for animals and travellers, and it is one of the better preserved caravanserais in the country.

Around it lie sand dunes that can reach respectable heights, and a little further the Namak, the salt lake, whose crust shines white and pink in low light. The silence is heavy, and a short walk away from the road makes it complete. Camels roam in the area, and at dusk the sky is the sort you only get far from city lights.

The riding is about preparation. The road to the caravanserai is paved, and if you take it slowly it is straightforward, but beyond it sand tracks start and a road bike has no business on them. Midsummer heat is dangerous, so aim for October to April, when the days are warm and the nights cold enough for a jacket. Wind can fill the air with dust, sometimes enough to hide the dunes entirely, and the visible hint is a brown haze on the horizon.

Both Aran and Bidgol are old towns with beautiful mud-brick quarters, hammams and big traditional houses that survive from the time when this was a rich place, and a stop there makes the ride a day rather than an errand. The oasis, the caravanserai and the salt are all pieces of the same old logic, the way people moved goods across a land that did not want to be crossed, and you can feel it better from a bike than from a car, with the air on your face and the empty road ahead.
t.zeynoddin@31.4,54.7:
The Zeynoddin caravanserai is a round, mud-brick fortress in the desert between Yazd and Kerman, built in the sixteenth century in the Safavid era on one of the old caravan routes of central Iran. Its walls curve like a drum, with two storeys of arched cells around a courtyard and towers on the outside, and the whole thing the colour of the sand it stands on. Travellers on this road, merchants with camels carrying silk, spices and carpets, would stop here for the night, because the next water and shade was a long way off. It is one of the caravanserais listed by UNESCO in 2023, and it has been restored so that visitors can sleep inside, in the same cells where traders once stabled their animals.

The land around is the edge of the Dasht-e Kavir, a very dry plateau where gravel plains and low brown hills extend to the horizon, and the sky is a hard blue. Days are hot, nights cold, and a clear evening shows more stars than you have seen in years. Mahriz, a small town some thirty kilometres away, is the nearest settlement, and Yazd, a famous desert city of wind towers and mud-brick lanes, lies to the north-west. The Persian qanat system, an underground channel network that brings water from the mountains, made life possible here.

For riders, the desert roads are long, straight and quiet, with slow curves over low passes and a lot of empty space. Surfaces are generally good on the main roads, but trucks are heavy, and the wind picks up sand and dust that may reduce visibility. Take plenty of water, sun protection and a spare layer for the nights. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, because midsummer reaches high forties and winter nights are freezing. Distances are great and services scarce, so fill the tank whenever you can.

Fuel is available in Mahriz and on the main highways, but check before heading off the main road. The caravanserai can serve a simple meal, and tea is always offered. Travel in Iran has its own rules and complications for visitors, and a motorcycle brings more, so check the conditions before you plan. If you get here, the evening sit in the courtyard, with the stone cooling and tea in your hand, is the point of the trip.
t.qanat of vazvan@33.4,51.2:
A qanat is a tunnel with a long memory. Somewhere in the foothills a digger sank a shaft until he struck water-bearing gravel, then cut a gently sloping tunnel from the water downhill to a village, with vertical shafts every few dozen metres to let in air and haul out spoil, so that water flowed to the surface by gravity alone, without a pump and without evaporating in the sun. The Persians were doing this by the first millennium BC, and the idea travelled to Egypt, North Africa and Spain. UNESCO listed eleven Persian qanats in 2016, and the one at Vazvan, in the province of Isfahan, is among them. It is still in use, and its tunnel, hand-dug and thousands of metres long, still feeds fields and gardens.

What you can expect is a line of small mounds across the plain, like a string of anthills, each the spoil heap around a shaft. From the air they look like beads on a thread. The diggers, called muqannis, were specialised families who handed on their skills, and the person in charge of the qanat, the mirab, shared the water out fairly among the users by the hour.

The country is the high plateau of central Iran, at roughly two thousand metres, with bare brown hills, wide gravel plains and green oases wherever the water arrives. The road between Isfahan and Kashan runs through this dry landscape, with long straights and low passes, and the mountains of the Zagros stand to the south-west. The air is thin and clear, and the evening light turns the hills pink and violet.

Riding on these roads is easy but remote. Surfaces are generally fine on the main routes, but trucks are heavy, and the wind raises dust. Villages are far apart, so carry water and fill the tank when you can, since fuel stops are spaced widely. Spring is best, when the plain is briefly green and the almond trees are in bloom, and autumn is also good. Summer is very hot, and winter can be snowy at this height. Check the rules for travel and for entering the country, which are complicated for visitors. A glass of sweet tea at a village stall is the best way to end the day.
t.abd alkuri a@12.2,52.1:
Socotra is the island everyone has heard of, with its dragon's blood trees and its upside-down umbrella shapes, but the archipelago has other members, and Abd al Kuri is the most western and the least visited. It lies about a hundred kilometres west of Socotra, closer to the Horn of Africa than to Yemen, and is a long, narrow slab of limestone and rock roughly thirty kilometres from end to end. Together with Socotra, Samha and Darsa, it forms a group that has been cut off from the mainland for millions of years, and that isolation has produced a remarkable number of species found nowhere else.

The geology tells part of the story. Socotra's islands are fragments of the old continental crust that broke away from Africa and Arabia, and Abd al Kuri is lower and drier than the main island, with a flat plateau, steep cliffs and small, scrubby valleys. Because of this, its vegetation is sparser, but it has its own rare plants and its own birds, among them a sparrow found only on the island. The seas around it are rich, and the waters hold turtles, dolphins and abundant fish.

Reaching it requires a boat from Socotra or the mainland, and the sea can be rough, particularly in the monsoon months of June to September, when the winds make crossings dangerous and often impossible. Yemen's political situation also makes travel to the region complicated, and conditions can change without warning, so any plan needs current advice from reliable sources and from people who know the islands.

If you are curious about the place, the best way to approach it is through the work of naturalists and the Socotra Conservation and Development Programme, whose writings are the best guide to what lives here. Supplies on the island are minimal, so anything you might need would have to be brought in, including water and fuel. It is a place that rewards patience, care and respect for the people who live there.
t.abd alkuri@12.2,52.2:
The people of Abd al Kuri are fishermen, and their lives follow the sea more than the land. The island is thinly populated, with a handful of small settlements, including Kilmia, a village on the coast, and the houses are low and simple, made of stone and cement, with boats drawn up on the beach. Fish, dried and salted, is the staple, along with goat meat, dates and rice brought from the mainland. The islanders speak a language related to the Socotri language of the main island, which is a South Arabian tongue that is quite different from Arabic and has no written tradition.

Daily life is dominated by the monsoon. From about June to September, the south-west wind drives heavy seas around the archipelago, boats stay on the beach, and the island is effectively cut off. In the calmer months, from October to May, fishing resumes, and the sea turns to a deep, glassy blue. Travellers who reach the islands in these months describe white sand beaches, turquoise water and extraordinary quiet. Socotra's famous hospitality extends to the smaller islands, and a visitor can expect to be offered tea and fish.

Anyone looking at a route that ends here should be honest about the practicalities. Access depends on boats, the rules for visiting change, and the wider political situation in Yemen makes travel there uncertain. If the label has come from a route-planning tool, treat it as a point on the map rather than a ride, and consider that the real experience is likely to be one of walking, boats and conversation.

Supplies are very limited. There is no reliable fuel for vehicles, and fresh water and food depend on what the village has and what boats bring in, so visitors must be self-sufficient and be careful not to burden a small community. The pleasure of such a place is the quiet, the sea, and the sense of being a very long way from anywhere, so take it slowly, ask permission before taking photographs of people, and leave nothing behind.

t.segment ranchillos@-32.6,-69.5:
Ranchillos lies in the Uspallata valley in Mendoza province, Argentina, on the high road that runs west from the city of Mendoza toward Chile. The valley is a broad, dry basin at about 1,900 metres between the Precordillera and the High Andes, with poplars along the river, scrubby desert and bare peaks banded in rust, yellow and green. The famous Ruta 7, the road to the Cristo Redentor pass and the border, runs through it, and people have travelled this corridor for a very long time.

That includes the Inca. The Qhapaq Ñan, their great road network, reached this part of the Andes, and the Argentine sections of the network are part of the 2014 UNESCO listing shared with five other countries. Ranchillos and the nearby Tambillos were stopping points, small tambos where travellers could rest and store supplies on the route over the Andes. Later, Spanish travellers, mule trains and eventually the railway used the same natural line, and you can see remains of the old railway in the valley today.

For a rider, this is one of the great Andean roads. Climbing from Mendoza, the road passes the reservoirs of Potrerillos, climbs through red canyons and arrives in Uspallata, where you can find fuel and food. Uspallata is a small town of a few thousand people and a handy base. Beyond it Ruta 7 rises past Puente del Inca, a natural rock bridge stained yellow by mineral springs, and Aconcagua comes into view, the highest mountain outside Asia at nearly 6,960 metres. The pass into Chile is regularly closed by snow or weather in winter, so check conditions and border status first.

The air is thin and dry, and the weather can change fast. The wind in Uspallata can be strong, and nights are cold even in summer, so layers are not optional. Sunshine is intense at this altitude, and the sky can be a deep, very clean blue. The valley was also used as a location for the film Seven Years in Tibet. Mendoza's malbec is the natural drink to look forward to, and a grilled asado with a glass of red is the classic reward at the end of the day.
t.rashti@32.4,53.6:
Rashti is a place name on a map of the central Iranian desert, and the honest thing to say is that it is a small, remote spot among the vast salt-and-gravel country that lies east of Isfahan. The nearest town of real size is Ardakan, about forty kilometres away, in Yazd province, and the closest settlement in the data is the village of Khavash Kuh. Beyond that, there is little for a long way in any direction except the sort of stony plain and low mountains that make up much of the Iranian plateau.

This is the edge of the Dasht-e Kavir, the great salt desert, and the landscape is austere and beautiful. The ground is pale, the sky enormous, and in the evening the hills turn rose and violet. People have lived here for millennia by tapping groundwater with qanats, underground channels that carry water from the mountains for kilometres to desert villages. The towns of Yazd province are famous for wind towers, called badgirs, which catch breezes and cool the houses below, and for their Zoroastrian communities and fire temples. Ardakan itself is an old town of mud-brick lanes and domed cisterns.

The riding is long and lonely. Roads cut across the plain in straight lines for tens of kilometres, with occasional curves around low hills, and the surface is generally decent on the main roads and rougher on the side ones. Wind and dust are constant, and in summer the heat is severe. Distances between fuel stations can be large, so fill the tank in Ardakan or Yazd and carry spare water. In winter nights can be below freezing, and the desert air is dry and clear.

Ardakan has about fifty-eight thousand people and has fuel, shops and food, including the Iranian staples of kebab, rice and flat bread with yogurt and herbs. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with warm days and cool nights. Carry plenty of water, a spare tube and a phone map, and tell someone where you are going.
t.bagh e chehel sotun@32.7,51.7:
Chehel Sotun means forty columns, and the name is a lovely piece of exaggeration, since the pavilion has twenty slender wooden pillars and the other twenty are their reflections in the long pool in front. It stands in a royal garden in the middle of Isfahan, a few hundred metres from the great square Naqsh-e Jahan, and was built in the seventeenth century under the Safavid shah Abbas II, who used it for receptions and banquets. The tall entrance porch, with its cedar columns inlaid with mirror and painted ceiling, is the setting for a famous scene: a royal audience with ambassadors seated on cushions in the shade, looking out over fountains and trees.

Inside are enormous wall paintings in the Persian style, showing the shah at feasts and in battle, and the grand reception hall holds scenes of a victory over the Uzbeks and another over the Mughals, painted with such careful detail that you can study the costumes of both sides. Look for the smaller panels showing a more private world, of wine bearers and dancers in graceful poses. The palace burned in the eighteenth century, and some of the paintings were later restored or painted over, but the effect remains rich. It is one of the nine Persian Gardens listed by UNESCO.

Isfahan itself is a city of about one and a half million people and a joy to explore, with its covered bazaar, the Imam Mosque with its blue tiles, the Lotfollah Mosque and the old bridges over the Zayandeh river, which is sometimes dry, sometimes full, depending on the season. The city is flat, and the boulevards are lined with plane trees, but traffic is a challenge. Drivers are fast and flexible about lanes, motorbikes weave through gaps, and pedestrians cross anywhere. Ride defensively and expect surprises at roundabouts.

Parking near the garden is possible on side streets, and the entrance is inexpensive. Spring is the best season, when the roses are in flower and the days are mild. Summer is hot and dry, and winter can be cold and clear. There are fuel stations on every main road and a wide choice of restaurants, with Isfahani specialities such as beryani, a spiced minced-meat dish, and gaz, a nougat flavoured with pistachios and rose. Come in the late afternoon and you can sit by the pool as the sun lowers and the columns glow.
t.area 3@31.9,54.4:
Yazd was listed by UNESCO as a whole city, and the listing divides the historic town into numbered zones, which is where labels like Area 3 come from. The walls are the colour of the desert, the roofs are domed to shed heat, and above the skyline stand rows of badgirs, the wind towers that catch the faintest breeze and push it down into the rooms below, a form of air conditioning that has worked for centuries.

Walking is the way to see it, and a motorbike is best parked at the edge of the old quarter. The lanes are only a couple of metres wide, roofed in places by arches and dark tunnels, with sudden turns and doors set at the side of blank walls. Many of the old houses have been turned into small hotels and teahouses, built around courtyards with a pool in the middle and rooms opening onto a shaded iwan. Look up and you will find fine plaster ceilings and painted glass in coloured windows, which throw patches of red and green light across the floor.

Yazd lies between two great deserts, the Dasht-e Kavir and the Dasht-e Lut, and the climate is blistering in summer and sharp in winter, with very little rain. The city lives from water brought in by qanats, which come from the mountains to the south-west, and a water museum in a historic house tells the story.

The outskirts have fuel stations and a modern city of nearly half a million people, with traffic that behaves rather more calmly than in Tehran or Isfahan. Taft, about twenty-three kilometres away, is a small town in the foothills with orchards, and makes a pleasant excursion. Try the local sweets, especially baklava and ghotab, an almond-filled pastry, and the cardamom cakes sold in shops around the old bazaar. Carry water even for a short walk, and wear light clothes that cover arms and legs, both for the sun and for local customs.
t.area 1@31.9,54.4:
When UNESCO listed the Historic City of Yazd in 2017 it described a living desert town of earthen architecture, and the zones in the description, such as Area 1, divide the old city into parts for protection. The mosque, begun in the twelfth century and added to over the next three, has one of the highest entrance portals in Iran, and the dome inside is a cool, blue-tiled cavern.

From the rooftops you can see how the old city is built, with a continuous skyline of domes, flat roofs and wind towers, and behind them the pale ridge of the Shirkuh mountains. Yazd was a stop on the caravan road between Isfahan and Kerman, and merchants brought silk, cotton and carpets through its gates. Marco Polo visited in the thirteenth century and called it a good and noble city, which still sounds right. The city is also a centre of the Zoroastrian faith, with a fire temple whose flame is said to have burned for more than fifteen centuries, and the dry hills outside the city still hold the Towers of Silence, where the dead were once left to the vultures.

Practicalities are simple. Use the edge of the old town for parking, since the lanes are narrow, and walk. Early morning is the quietest time, and the sun in the lanes is low and soft. The bazaar is covered, cool and full of copper pots, textiles and sweets, and you can bargain in a friendly way. Tea houses on the roofs serve tea and kalian, the water pipe, with a view across the domes, and sunset there is memorable, as the call to prayer drifts out.

Fuel is available along the ring road, and the city is large enough for every service, including spares and mechanics. In summer it is very hot, so plan sightseeing before ten in the morning and after five in the evening. Dress modestly, with long sleeves and trousers, and women should carry a scarf. Take plenty of water, and if you have energy left, ride out to Meybod, a small town with an old citadel and a pigeon tower, about an hour north-west.
t.kuhpayeh@32.7,52.4:
The road east from Isfahan goes on for a long time without a great deal to look at, and Kuhpayeh is one of the places that breaks the journey. The name means foot of the mountain, and it is an old oasis town in Isfahan province where the Zayandeh river's last water and a network of canals have kept orchards and fields alive at the edge of the desert, with low brown hills behind.

The Zayandeh is the river of Isfahan, rising in the Zagros mountains and flowing east across the plateau, and the people of the region have depended on it for centuries. Its fate is a modern worry, because irrigation and drought have left it dry for long periods, and the great marsh at its end, Gavkhuni, shrinks and expands with the years. Farmers on the lower stretches have seen their water dwindle, and a visit in the dry season shows the cracked bed and the ghosts of old channels.

For a rider, the highways of this region are fast and straight, lined with truck stops, with big views of salt flats and ridges. Wind is common, and the sun on the road can be punishing in summer. The best time is spring, when the orchards flower and the desert air is clear, or October, when temperatures drop. After dark, trucks, animals and unlit vehicles are hazards, so aim to arrive in daylight.

Fuel is available at stations along the main highway, but it is worth topping up in Isfahan and again at any station you trust, because queues and supply problems do occur. Roadside restaurants serve grilled kebab with rice and grilled tomatoes, with raw onions and a glass of doogh, and the owners may offer a mat in the shade to sleep on at midday. Pistachio and dried-fruit stalls sell by the kilo. Carry water and sun protection, and plan your day so that you are not riding in the heat of the afternoon.
t.historic city of yazd@31.9,54.4:
Marco Polo passed through Yazd in the thirteenth century and called it a good and noble city, which is high praise from a man who had seen a great deal. It is the largest city in the world built mostly of adobe, a pale, soft, sun-baked mud brick, and it lies in the middle of Iran, shut in by two deserts and the Shirkuh range. That isolation is what saved it. When invaders swept across the plateau, Yazd's remoteness, and the money to pay them off, helped it survive, and the Zoroastrians, followers of Iran's ancient pre-Islamic religion, found a refuge here that they still hold.

The city's genius is its response to heat and dryness. The qanats bring water from the hills, the houses are built around courtyards with deep cellars called sardabs, and the streets are narrow so that the buildings shade each other. Wind towers catch the breeze, and some of the old ice houses, great conical domes outside the walls, stored winter ice for use in summer. The brickwork, with its patterns of shadows, looks almost carved, and the soft light at the end of the day turns the walls the colour of honey.

Beyond the old town, Yazd has some remarkable places, including the Amir Chakhmaq complex, a three-storey facade of arched niches that lights up at night, and the Zoroastrian fire temple with its flame behind glass. About twenty kilometres from the city stands Chak Chak, a mountain shrine where water drips from a rock face, which is a pilgrimage place for Zoroastrians each June. Roads to the surrounding villages cross desert plains and pass dunes, and the road to Meybod and Kharanaq makes a good loop.

In the city itself, traffic is calmer than in other Iranian cities, and a motorbike is easy to park. Fuel is plentiful, with several stations on the ring road, and hotels in old houses offer courtyards for secure parking. The cuisine includes a lamb stew with dried fruit, saffron rice with barberries, and the sweets of Yazd, such as pashmak, a spun-sugar floss, and qottab, a deep-fried almond pastry. Drink tea with sugar cubes, the local way, held in the teeth.
t.bagh e dolat abad@31.9,54.4:
Dolat Abad is the garden that gave the world a record: its wind tower is about thirty-three metres tall, among the tallest in the world, a hexagonal brick shaft rising above the pavilion of the old governor's house. It was laid out in the 1740s for Mohammad Taqi Khan, a local ruler under the Afsharid kings, and later enlarged under Karim Khan Zand, the gentle ruler of southern Iran. The garden is another of the nine Persian Gardens listed by UNESCO, and it shows the classic design: long avenues of cypress, a central axis of water, and a pavilion at the end that looks down the whole length.

The beauty of the pavilion is in the details. Inside, the main hall has windows of coloured glass in lattice frames, which throw jewelled light across the floor, and walls decorated with delicate paintings and plasterwork. A hall at the back opens beneath the wind tower, and in summer the cooling effect is remarkable. A small pool of water at the base cools the air passing down the shaft, and the room stays pleasant while the garden outside bakes. You can feel the breeze on your face. It is an object lesson in how to build a house for a desert.

The garden's water comes from a qanat that runs below the site, feeding a long, shallow channel lined with fountains. The cypresses along the axis are very old, planted in tall, dark rows that frame the pavilion. Pomegranate, grape and mulberry trees fill the beds, and in spring the smell of blossom mixes with the warm scent of earth. It is a good place to sit in the shade and watch the light move across the leaves.

The garden lies close to the old city, so riding there is easy. Parking is possible near the gate, and the surrounding streets are wide and quiet compared with those of the bazaar. Visit early in the morning, when the air is cool and the light is soft, or late in the afternoon, when the tour groups have gone. Fuel and food are plentiful in Yazd, and the nearby teahouses are good for a rest. In summer, take water and a hat, and in winter bring a jacket.
t.subsection cienaga de yalguaraz san albe:
Between the provinces of San Juan and Mendoza, the Andes of western Argentina stand up as a dry, enormous wall, and this stretch lies in their rain shadow, where the land is a mix of high steppe, stony ridges and green strips of irrigated valley. The air is clear and thin, the sky is a deep, flat blue, and the sun is fierce even in winter. To the south-west, over the border ridge, stands Aconcagua, the highest mountain in the Americas at almost seven thousand metres, though you will not always see it for the haze.

The label here refers to part of the Qhapaq Ñan, the Inca road system that UNESCO listed in 2014, and the segment runs from a place called Ciénaga de Yalguaraz toward San Albert. A ciénaga is a marsh, a patch of wet ground that in a dry landscape is worth more than gold, and it is no surprise that travellers have always used such places as stops. The Incas pushed their road south into what is now Argentina and Chile, and archaeologists have traced stone-lined paths, storage buildings and way stations in these valleys. Before and after the Incas, the same routes carried herders, muleteers and the armies of San Martín, who in 1817 crossed the Andes to free Chile from Spanish rule in one of the great mountain marches of history.

The riding here is the long, open kind. Roads climb gently up broad valleys, with big views, then wind through narrow canyons where the rock walls are stained red and green by minerals. Surfaces vary, from smooth tarmac on main routes to rough gravel on side tracks, and after summer storms flash floods wash across the road in washes and dry gullies. Wind builds in the afternoon, and the cold at night can be startling after a hot day. A warm layer, spare water and a reliable map are the basics.

The sensible plan is to take fuel and food at one of the bigger centres, such as Calingasta, Uspallata or Mendoza itself, and to carry more than you think you need. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with clear light and moderate temperatures, and high passes can close with snow between May and October, so check before you go.
t.bonaventure@48.0,-65.5:
Bonaventure sits on the southern shore of the Gaspé Peninsula, on the Baie des Chaleurs, the Bay of Heat, whose waters are among the warmest in the Gulf of St Lawrence, and its sheltered beaches are popular for swimming in summer. The town was founded in 1760 by Acadian refugees, who had fled the British deportation of their people and found shelter in this quiet bay. The Musée acadien du Québec, in the town, tells the story with objects, documents and a gentle, human touch. The Acadian flag, a French tricolour with a yellow star, flies from many houses.

The Bonaventure River, a clear, fast river known for salmon fishing, runs through the town to the sea, and it is a favourite for canoeists and anglers. The surrounding hills are covered in spruce and fir, and fields run down to the shore, with fishing boats and old wharves. The bay stretches away to the south, and on a clear day you can see the New Brunswick coast across the water.

Route 132, the road that circles the Gaspé Peninsula, passes through Bonaventure and is a classic coastal ride, with sea views, villages, red-roofed churches and long, easy bends. The surface is generally good, though frost heaves can make some stretches bumpy. The ride from Gaspé to Bonaventure, passing Percé and its great rock, is spectacular, and the quiet end at Bonaventure is a gentle reward. The traffic is light outside July and August.

Bonaventure has about two and a half thousand people, with a fuel station, a supermarket, a handful of restaurants and several places to stay. Seafood is excellent, with fresh lobster, scallops and smoked salmon on offer, and a plate of fish and chips beside the water is hard to beat. The weather can be foggy and cool, even in summer, and the evenings are chilly, so bring a warm layer. Take time to walk on the beach and watch the sun go down over the bay.
t.rimouski@48.4,-68.5:
Rimouski stands on the south shore of the St. Lawrence, where the river has widened into an estuary so broad that the far shore, forty kilometres away, is a blue line of mountains. The sea is only a taste of salt and a tide here, but it changes the weather, the light and the character of the town. About forty-two thousand people live in this lively regional capital of the Bas-Saint-Laurent, with a university, a long waterfront and the unhurried feel of a place that most visitors pass through on the way to somewhere further east.

The story people remember is a sad one. In May 1914, in thick fog, the liner Empress of Ireland was struck by a collier in the river just off Pointe-au-Père, a few kilometres east of town, and sank in about fourteen minutes. More than a thousand people died, a toll that few people outside Canada seem to know. A museum at the point tells the story, and next to it you can walk through an old submarine. The lighthouse beside them, one of the tallest in the country, is open to visitors in season.

For the rider, Rimouski is the gateway to the Gaspé Peninsula and Route 132, which follows the river for hundreds of kilometres. The road eastwards is a ribbon of villages, white churches with silver spires, fishing wharves and farms, with the Laurentians or the Chic-Chocs rising across the water or up ahead. The surface is generally good, though it has frost heaves and patched stretches, and the weather can turn quickly: fog is common, and the wind off the river can be sharp. Summer and early autumn are the best times, when days are long and the sea air is mild.

Rimouski has everything: fuel stations, supermarkets, small hotels and a string of seafood restaurants, and the larger town is the last good chance for services before the long coast of the Gaspé. In Quebec, the local specialities include smoked fish, maple products, strong cheese and poutine, and the roadside stands in summer sell fresh strawberries. Signs are in French, distances are in kilometres, and speed limits are enforced on the main road, so keep an eye on the limits through the villages.
t.sainte anne des monts@49.1,-66.5:
Sainte-Anne-des-Monts is the gateway to the Gaspésie National Park, on the north coast of the Gaspé Peninsula, where the St Lawrence River widens into the Gulf and the Chic-Chocs mountains rise abruptly behind the shore. The town is a pleasant, working place of about five and a half thousand people, with a church, a fishing wharf and a main street running along the coast. Behind it, the road to the park climbs into the mountains, where a herd of woodland caribou, the last south of the St Lawrence, survives on the high plateaus.

The park contains the highest peaks in southern Quebec, including Mont Jacques-Cartier and Mont Albert, with arctic-alpine vegetation, deep valleys and cold, clear rivers. Moose are common, and a road through the park offers a good chance to see them at dawn and dusk. The hiking trails are excellent, and a day spent among the mountains is a fine counterpoint to the coastal ride.

Route 132 runs along the shore, with sea views, small villages and white lighthouses, and it is one of the great coastal rides in eastern Canada. The surface is generally good, with long curves and some steeper sections where the mountains meet the sea. The traffic is light outside summer, and the wind off the Gulf can be strong and cold. Nearby Cap-Chat has a giant wind turbine, called Éole, which was the tallest vertical-axis turbine in the world, shaped like an egg-whisk and rising over a hundred metres.

Sainte-Anne-des-Monts has fuel stations, supermarkets, restaurants and places to stay, and it is a sensible stop on the long run around the peninsula. Seafood is the local speciality, with shrimp, crab and fresh fish served at harbour-side restaurants. The weather can be cool and foggy, even in summer, and nights are cold, so carry warm clothing. In the evening, with the sun setting over the water and the mountains turning pink, the place is quietly magnificent.
t.the persian garden@30.2,53.2:
The Persian garden is an idea as much as a place: a rectangle of shade and water in a dry land, divided into four parts by channels that stand for the rivers of paradise. The word paradise itself comes from an old Persian word for an enclosed garden. This one, near Pasargadae, belongs to a group of nine gardens across Iran that are listed together by UNESCO, and it is the earliest of them, laid out by Cyrus the Great in the sixth century BC beside his new capital.

Little survives except the bones of the design. Limestone channels, pools and basins, set in a pattern of straight lines, can still be traced among the pavilions, and they show how the engineers moved water across the plain, using gravity to carry it from springs and streams. In the dry air of the Fars plateau, a garden with running water was a statement of power, and the effect, with trees casting shade over cool pools, must have been dazzling.

The nearest town, Pasargad, is four kilometres away, and has fuel, a few small shops and tea houses. Shiraz, with its markets and its famous gardens, is about a hundred and thirty kilometres to the south-west. The road across the plain is long and straight, with views of mountains on both sides. At about nineteen hundred metres above sea level, the air is cool at night and in winter, and the sun is strong in summer.

Come in spring or autumn, when the temperatures are mild, and bring water and a hat. Early morning, when the light is soft and the plain is quiet, is the best time to walk among the old channels. The garden is a place to sit and consider how a people with little water made a paradise out of it, and how that idea travelled to the Alhambra, the Taj Mahal and a thousand courtyards in between.
t.pasargadae@30.2,53.2:
Pasargadae was the first capital of the Persian empire, founded by Cyrus the Great after his defeat of the Median king around 550 BC. It stands on the plain of Morghab in southern Iran, at an altitude of about nineteen hundred metres, and the setting is one of wide, open space, bounded by low mountains. The tomb of Cyrus, a plain stone chamber on a six-stepped base, stands alone in the grass, and its simplicity is striking, given that it holds the founder of the largest empire the world had yet seen.

According to the Greek historians, Alexander the Great visited the tomb and was moved by its modesty, and ordered it restored after it had been looted. The inscription, if it ever existed, is lost. Elsewhere on the site, you can see the ruins of palaces and a gateway guarded by a winged figure, and the foundations of a tower. The Cyrus Cylinder, a clay cylinder found in Babylon, records the king's policy of respect for the customs of conquered peoples, and has been described as an early charter of tolerance, though historians argue about the claim.

The town of Pasargad, a kilometre and a half away, has about 30,000 people, with fuel, shops and simple restaurants, and the site itself has a small ticket office and car park. Persepolis, the later capital of Darius, lies about fifty kilometres to the south, and the two are often visited together. The road between them crosses a high, dry plain with fields of wheat, barley and pomegranate trees.

Visit in spring, when the grass is green, or in autumn, when the light is golden and the heat has eased. Winters are cold, and summers are baking, with little shade. Take water and a hat, and walk slowly. At sunset the stone of the tomb glows warm, and the wind in the grass makes a sound like quiet voices.
t.samara@53.2,50.1:
The Volga makes a great bend at Samara, and the city sits at its elbow. Here the river, nearly a kilometre wide, swings around the Zhiguli Mountains, a long ridge of forested hills that is the only real high ground for hundreds of kilometres in any direction. The mountains form a peninsula inside the loop, known as the Samara Bend, and its cliffs, caves and pine woods are among the best riding country in the Volga region. The city holds more than a million people and spreads along the left bank.

Samara has a strange history. In 1941, with Moscow threatened, it was made the reserve capital of the Soviet Union and renamed Kuibyshev, and diplomats and government offices moved here. Stalin's bunker, built deep underground, still exists and can be visited. The embankment, one of the longest in Russia at about four and a half kilometres, is a fine place for an evening walk, with sandy beaches and views across the river. The city is also known for beer: the Zhigulevskoye brand dates from a brewery founded in the nineteenth century by an Austrian, Alfred von Vacano.

North of the city, the painter Ilya Repin spent a summer in 1870 at the village of Shiryaevo, sketching the barge haulers who pulled boats up the Volga, which became his famous painting. The cliffs there are a classic view, and the road to the village winds through fields and woodland. Further into the bend, roads climb through forest with bends and short climbs, passing old kurgans and viewpoints over the water. Surfaces vary, and trucks use the main roads, so choose side roads for a quieter ride.

Fuel and food are plentiful in the city, and smaller places such as Novokuybyshevsk and Rozhdestveno have basics. Summers are hot and dry, winters are cold and snowy, and the best season runs from May to September. Foreign riders should check what is currently possible before planning travel.
t.millinocket@45.7,-68.7:
Millinocket is the last town before the woods. The name is Abenaki and the place has the air of a frontier, with a long main street, a few cafes and a big skyline of wooded hills behind. For most of the twentieth century it was a mill town, built around the paper mills of the Great Northern Paper Company, which gave it the title Magic City of the Maine Woods, but the mills closed in the 2000s, and the town has been reinventing itself since as a base for outdoor travel.

The reason to come is Katahdin. This great granite massif, at 1,606 metres the highest point in Maine, rises abruptly from flat forest and lakes and is the northern end of the Appalachian Trail, which starts in Georgia, some 3,500 kilometres away. Baxter State Park surrounds it, with strict rules, limited numbers and gravel roads, and entry for non-residents costs a fee. To the east, Katahdin Woods and Waters National Monument was created in 2016 on land donated by Roxanne Quimby, and its loop road runs through spruce, fir and birch with views across the Penobscot River valley to the mountain.

For motorcyclists, the pavement runs out fast. The main road from town to Baxter's Togue Pond gate is paved, but inside the park the roads are gravel, narrow and slow, and the same goes for the loop in the monument. Moose, bears and logging trucks share the way, and rain can turn the surface greasy. Black flies from late May to June can be miserable, and the best months are July to September, with the leaves turning in late September.

Millinocket has fuel, groceries, motels and diners, and East Millinocket, eleven kilometres away, has a little more. Beyond, services are sparse, so fill up and carry food. Mist often lies over the Penobscot at dawn, and the view of Katahdin glowing pink at sunrise from the lake edge is worth rising for.
t.mendoza@-32.9,-68.8:
Mendoza is a city of trees. Walk or ride any of its wide avenues and you will pass under rows of old plane trees, fed by narrow irrigation channels called acequias, a system that the indigenous Huarpe people started long before the Spanish arrived. The reason is the desert: Mendoza gets very little rain, and every green leaf here exists because snowmelt from the Andes is carried down in channels and spread across the plain. It is a city of nearly nine hundred thousand people in the greater area, set against a wall of mountains that, on a clear winter morning, includes the white shoulder of Aconcagua far to the west.

An earthquake in 1861 flattened most of the colonial town, and the planners who rebuilt it did so with wide streets and open plazas so that people could flee into the open next time. That gives the centre a spacious, calm feeling, with Plaza Independencia as its heart, and cafes spilling onto the pavement under the shade. For a rider arriving on a loaded bike, the traffic is orderly by South American standards, though buses, taxis and drivers who ignore their indicators call for alertness.

The ride from here is a wine ride. Malbec is the grape that made the region famous, and the vineyards of Luján de Cuyo, Maipú and the higher Uco Valley produce some of the best. The roads between the bodegas are flat and straight, lined with poplars, with the Andes on the horizon, and the mood is more of a gentle roll than a hard ride. Many bodegas offer tastings and lunch by appointment, and as a rider you will want to take that slowly, or just buy a bottle for later.

Ruta 7 leads west toward the mountains and eventually to the Chilean border via Uspallata, a spectacular road that climbs to the Cristo Redentor tunnel region and the foot of Aconcagua. In winter, snow can close the border crossing for days.

Fuel is plentiful in the city and along the main roads, and the choice of food is excellent, from empanadas to long beef grills. Summer is hot and dry, so start early. Autumn, with the vines turning red and gold, is the finest time of year to be here.
t.hanmer springs@-42.5,172.8:
Hanmer Springs is a small alpine village in the Hurunui district of north Canterbury, set in a broad basin among forested hills about an hour and a half's drive from the Pacific coast. The hot springs here were found by European settlers in the 1850s and have been in use ever since, and the thermal pools at the centre of the village, with their rock pools, sulphur baths and water slides, are what draw most visitors. Around them the village has cafes, restaurants, a handful of shops and a long list of places to stay, and about a thousand people live here year-round.

The village is also the gateway to the Molesworth Station road, the long gravel track between Hanmer Springs and Blenheim that crosses what is said to be New Zealand's largest farm. The road follows the Acheron and Awatere valleys through a vast, empty high country of tussock hills, mountains and braided rivers, and it is open to the public only in the summer months, usually from around December to April, with a small fee. In winter it is closed. If you plan to ride it, check the dates and conditions with the local information centre.

So fill up in Hanmer Springs before you leave, since the next reliable pump is in Blenheim, a long way off. Pack water and a few snacks. The countryside is arid and bare, and it feels huge, with the Kaikoura ranges standing at the edge of the view. The route is an old stock road and later a supply road to the station, and you see the old huts and yards along the way.

Back in the village, there are walks in the forest park, where the larch and redwood stands planted in the early twentieth century make a good place to spend an hour. The thermal pools are a fine way to finish a ride, especially on a cold evening in autumn, and soaking tired shoulders after a day on gravel is one of the great pleasures of the South Island.
t.punakaiki@-42.1,171.3:
Punakaiki sits on a short stretch of the West Coast where the Paparoa Range comes down almost to the sea, and the combination of green rainforest, limestone cliffs and Tasman breakers makes it one of the most photographed places on State Highway 6. The village itself is tiny, with a handful of cafes, a visitor centre and some accommodation, but it has one very big attraction, the Pancake Rocks, a set of limestone formations that look like piles of stacked pancakes, shaped over thousands of years from layers of soft and hard sediment eroded by sea and rain.

The rocks are the best known feature, and the blowholes beside them are even more dramatic. When a big swell comes in at high tide, the sea forces itself into the caves under the rocks and shoots up through vertical shafts in a roar of spray and thunder, and a short boardwalk lets you stand beside them. Check the tide tables, since a low tide in a calm sea makes the show a little disappointing. The nikau palms, which are New Zealand's only native palm, grow in the forest here, giving the scene a surprisingly subtropical look.

The riding on this section of SH6 is a pleasure. The road follows the coast with long open bends, glimpses of surf, rocky headlands and thick bush, and it is mostly well surfaced, with a few narrow one-lane bridges where you give way. Traffic is steady in summer, but the road is wide enough for a bike. The weather is the main variable, because the West Coast is one of the wettest parts of the country and rain can come in sheets, followed by sunshine and a rainbow.

t.socotra g@12.3,54.0:
Socotra's south coast feels like the far side of a very strange moon. Here the island drops from the granite spine of the Haggier mountains onto a broad gravel plain that runs down to a hot, wind-scoured shore, with dunes piled against the cliffs and nothing taller than a goat for miles.

The island has been cut off from mainland Africa and Arabia for millions of years, and it shows. A third of its plants grow nowhere else: the dragon's blood tree with its umbrella of stiff branches, the swollen desert rose that looks like a bottle stuck in rock, frankincense and myrrh clinging to bare limestone. UNESCO listed the archipelago in 2008 for exactly this. On the southern side you also get the island's great sand drifts, pale and smooth against dark mountains, which turn honey coloured in the hour before sunset.

Be honest with yourself about logistics. Socotra belongs to Yemen, a country at war, and most governments advise against travel; the few visitors who come arrive on limited flights and almost always travel with a local guide and driver. Very few riders bring their own machine, and the realistic way to see the south is from the seat of a hired four-wheel drive or a borrowed local motorbike. The road from Hadibu crosses the mountains and is paved in places, rough in others, and the summer monsoon from roughly June to September brings gales strong enough to stop traffic and halt flights.

Fill every tank and can in Hadibu and treat water the same way, carrying more than you think. Food is whatever your guide arranges, usually rice, fresh fish grilled on the beach and goat, with sweet tea brewed over a driftwood fire. Camping under that southern sky, with no lights between you and Somalia, is one of the quiet, rare privileges of travel.
t.socotra b@12.6,53.8:

Both towns lie roughly thirty kilometres away in opposite directions, which makes the place a natural midpoint on the island's main east–west journey.

What makes the north coast special is the view up. Look inland and the plateaus are scattered with bottle trees and cucumber trees, while beyond them the jagged granite of the Haggier range catches cloud most afternoons. In the right season the wadis carry clear water down to the shore, and you can stop by a pool where small fish dart around your boots while Egyptian vultures watch from the rocks. The birdlife is outstanding, with several species found only on the archipelago.

People have lived here for a very long time, trading frankincense and aloe with Greek, Indian and Arab sailors. The islanders speak Soqotri, an ancient South Arabian language that has no traditional written form and that linguists are working hard to record. Life still turns on goats, dates and the sea, and the courtesy shown to visitors is old-fashioned and sincere. Dress modestly, ask before photographing people and accept the tea when it is offered.

Practicalities are simple and stark. Yemen remains under travel warnings, so visits usually come through organised trips with local guides, and private vehicles are rare. t.socotra b@12.7,53.6:

Life here revolves around fishing, and in the early morning you can watch the boats come in loaded with tuna and reef fish, while children play in the shallows and goats nose through the nets.

The calm waters around the west also hold coral reefs and rich marine life, especially in the months when the sea is flat. Yemen's long conflict means most governments advise against travel, and visits are typically organised through local operators, with guides and drivers who know the island well.

The road west from Hadibu is paved, but sand drifts across it, and beyond Qalansiya tracks quickly become rough. Fuel is available in Hadibu, and sometimes in Qalansiya, so plan carefully. t.kharanaq@32.3,54.7:
