Kharanaq is an old village, its oldest parts often said to be more than a thousand years old, largely abandoned by its residents when they moved to newer houses down the slope. Walking through it is like entering a sandcastle on a giant scale, with narrow covered passages, tiny rooms, wooden doors and the sound of wind whistling through holes in the walls.

Several buildings stand out. A slim minaret, famous for gently swaying when pushed or climbed, rises beside the old mosque. A restored caravanserai sits below the village, a reminder that Kharanaq lay on routes that brought travellers across the desert towards Yazd, and an old aqueduct and the remains of water channels show how carefully the inhabitants managed every drop. Restoration work has brought some buildings back to life as guesthouses and cafés, keeping the place from slipping entirely into ruin.

The road to Kharanaq leaves the Yazd plain and climbs into bare, rocky hills, an hour or so north of Yazd itself, passing through Ardakan country and the hard, sunburnt landscape of the central plateau. The tarmac is generally good, with long, empty straights across gravel plains and a few winding sections as the road enters the valley. Wind can be fierce, carrying sand and dust, and in summer the heat is relentless, so April and October are the months to choose, with the low evening light turning the village gold.

Bring fuel from Yazd or Ardakan, where stations are plentiful, and carry plenty of water, as services in the hills are sparse. Yazd itself is a wonderful city of wind towers, Zoroastrian fire temples and mud-brick lanes, and it makes the obvious base. Riding conditions in Iran come with their own rules: regulations for motorcycles, particularly larger ones, can be restrictive, so check the current situation carefully before planning a trip, and be aware that cultural expectations around dress apply to riders too.
t.area 2@31.9,54.4:
Yazd is a city built to survive the desert, and riding into it you feel the logic of every wall. It sits on the dry central plateau of Iran between the Dasht-e Kavir and the Dasht-e Lut, and its old quarter is a maze of mud-brick lanes, domes and covered passages, with badgirs, the tall windcatcher towers, rising above the roofs to catch any breath of moving air and pull it down into the houses. UNESCO listed the historic city in 2017, and it is one of the oldest continuously inhabited towns in the country.

Water made Yazd possible. Qanats, underground channels dug by hand from the foot of the mountains to the south, carried groundwater for kilometres under the desert to the city, and some still run. You can go down into one at a water museum in town. Yazd is also the heart of Iran's Zoroastrian community: the Atash Behram fire temple keeps a flame said to have been burning for well over a thousand years, and on the edge of the city stand the Towers of Silence, the low round hills where the dead were once left for the vultures. The Jameh Mosque, with its twin minarets and tiled portal, anchors the old town.

Riding here is a lesson in heat and distance. The roads approaching Yazd are long, straight and well surfaced, crossing plains of gravel and sand with mountains floating in the haze. Summer temperatures are brutal, so ride early, rest through the afternoon and carry far more water than you think. Sand can drift onto the road in wind, and the city traffic is dense and unpredictable, with motorbikes going in every direction. Towards Taft and the Shir Kuh mountains to the southwest, the road climbs into greener, cooler villages with orchards.

Fuel in Iran is cheap but rationed by card for locals, so foreign riders should plan ahead and ask at stations; in a city of half a million people the stations themselves are easy to find. Yazd is famous for its sweets, especially baklava and cotton-candy-like pashmak, and its old-town courtyard guesthouses are wonderful places to rest under the shade of a pomegranate tree. Dress codes apply, so cover up when off the bike.
t.meybod@32.2,54.0:
Meybod is the kind of desert town that rewards anyone who slows down instead of rushing on to Yazd, fifty-odd kilometres to the southeast. It lies on the old road across the central Iranian plateau, a low sprawl of mud-brick and newer concrete with the Shir Kuh mountains on one horizon and nothing but gravel plain on the other, and it has been a waypoint for travellers for a very long time. Ardakan, its twin town, is just up the road.

The heart of the old town is Narin Qal'eh, a mud-brick citadel on a mound that may go back to pre-Islamic times, with layered walls rising like a sandcastle above the roofs. From the top you see the whole logic of a desert settlement: the old quarters huddled together for shade, the gardens fed by qanats, and the long empty road. Close by stand some of the best-preserved pieces of old Persian infrastructure anywhere: a caravanserai built for merchants and their camels, a chaparkhaneh or royal post station where couriers changed horses, a domed yakhchal or ice house in which winter ice was stored through the summer, and a pigeon tower that collected droppings for fertiliser. Seeing them side by side, a few hundred metres apart, is like walking through a diagram of how people lived here.

Meybod is also known for its ceramics, with blue and turquoise glazed bowls and plates made in workshops around town, and for zilu, a flat-woven cotton rug with simple geometric patterns, traditionally woven for mosques. Buying a small piece is easy, and the workshops are often happy to show you the looms.

Riding in, the main road from Yazd is wide, fast and straight, with heavy lorries and long hot stretches where the mirage dances over the tarmac. There is little shade and the wind can carry sand, so a scarf for the face and goggles or a closed visor help. The town is a reasonable size, over fifty thousand people, so fuel stations, small restaurants and shops are easy to find, though as a foreigner you may need help at the pump with the fuel card system. Spring and autumn are the sensible seasons; in high summer, ride at dawn and spend the afternoon in the cool of the caravanserai, which now hosts a teahouse.
t.gaz@32.8,51.6:
Gaz is a town on the northern edge of the Isfahan plain, close to Shahin Shahr, and most riders pass through it on the way to or from Isfahan itself, about twenty kilometres to the south. The name makes Iranians smile, because gaz is also the word for Isfahan's beloved nougat, a soft white sweet studded with pistachios and made with a resin from the tamarisk shrub. Whatever the etymology, buying a box from one of the confectioners in the region is close to compulsory.

The landscape here is high, dry and flat, about fifteen hundred metres above sea level, with brown mountains rising on the horizon and farmland where water allows. That water, for most of history, came through qanats, the hand-dug underground channels that carry groundwater from aquifers at the mountain foot down to the fields, sometimes over many kilometres. The Persian qanat system is on the UNESCO list as a group of eleven examples, and one of them, the Mozd Abad qanat, is in this part of the Isfahan region. From the road you can sometimes spot the lines of shafts, little craters of excavated earth marching across the plain.

Isfahan is the big reward. Its Naqsh-e Jahan Square, also called Meidan Emam, was laid out by Shah Abbas I in the early seventeenth century as the centrepiece of his new capital, and it remains one of the largest and most beautiful city squares on earth, surrounded by the Shah Mosque, the Sheikh Lotfollah Mosque, the Ali Qapu palace and the entrance to the bazaar. The old bridges over the Zayandeh River, Si-o-se Pol and Khaju, are where the city comes to stroll in the evening, though the river itself has often been dry in recent years.

The riding between Gaz and Isfahan is urban highway: wide, busy and fast, with aggressive lane changes and a lot of motorbikes. Fuel is plentiful in Gaz, Dowlatabad and the surrounding towns, and there are plenty of kebab shops and bakeries selling fresh flatbread. The heat in summer is dry and strong, and in winter the plateau gets surprisingly cold at night, so pack for both ends of the thermometer. Ride into Isfahan in the late afternoon and you will arrive just as the square comes to life.
t.socotra a@12.7,53.5:
At the western tip of Socotra, near the fishing village of Qalansiyah, the island ends in a lagoon of almost unreal beauty. Detwah lagoon is a shallow basin of white sand and turquoise water, enclosed by dunes and limestone headlands, where fishermen pull up their boats on the beach and dolphins sometimes swim in the bay beyond. Socotra lies in the Arabian Sea, about three hundred and fifty kilometres off the coast of Yemen and closer to the Horn of Africa, and it has been isolated for so long that a large share of its plants and animals exist nowhere else on earth. UNESCO listed the archipelago in 2008 for its extraordinary biodiversity.

The most famous of its strange plants is the dragon's blood tree, shaped like an umbrella turned inside out, whose red resin has been traded since antiquity as a dye, medicine and varnish. There are also bottle trees, swollen and pink-flowered, growing out of rock, and cucumber trees, the only tree-sized member of the cucumber family. Birds include several endemic species, and the coral reefs offshore are rich with fish.

For riders, Socotra is a place to be honest about. The island has a handful of paved roads built in recent decades, linking Hadibu, the main town, to the airport and to Qalansiyah, and beyond those there are rough tracks into the mountains and along the coast. There is no realistic way to bring your own motorcycle here; visitors usually travel with a local driver and guide, and tourism is organised through a few operators. Yemen's long-running conflict means government travel advisories against visiting remain in place in many countries, so check carefully before planning anything.

Qalansiyah itself is a small village with a few shops; fuel and supplies are concentrated in Hadibu, at the other end of the island. The monsoon from June to September brings strong winds and rough seas that make the island hard to reach, and the best time to visit is from October to April. Camping on the beach at Detwah, under a sky full of stars, with the sound of the sea and the wind in the dunes, is unforgettable.
t.socotra d@12.7,54.1:
Hadibu is the main town of Socotra, a dusty, low-rise place on the north coast of the island, between the sea and the jagged granite peaks of the Hagghier mountains, which rise to around fifteen hundred metres just behind it. These mountains catch the clouds, and their slopes are greener and wetter than the coastal plains, with streams, pools and a remarkable range of endemic plants. The island's population is small, and Hadibu, with its market, mosques and goats wandering the streets, is the only real town.

Above Hadibu, the Homhil plateau is one of the best places to see the island's famous plants in their natural setting: dragon's blood trees perched on the cliff edges, frankincense trees with papery bark, and bottle trees growing out of the limestone, with a natural infinity pool at the edge of the plateau looking down to the sea. Further inland, the Dixam plateau and the Wadi Dirhur canyon have the densest forests of dragon's blood trees. The island's people speak Soqotri, an ancient language related to those of southern Arabia, and have traditionally lived from fishing, herding and date palms.

As at the other end of the island, the honest truth for riders is that Socotra is not a riding destination in the usual sense. You cannot ship your own bike in easily, roads beyond the main ones are rough tracks, and visits are generally arranged through local tour operators with drivers. The political situation in Yemen remains complex, with different authorities and foreign influences on the island, and many governments advise against travel. Check the latest information carefully.

If you do get here, Hadibu is where you will find fuel, simple restaurants serving grilled fish, rice and goat, and small shops. The coastline nearby has beautiful beaches and dunes, with white sand piled up against the mountains. The best season is between the monsoons, from October to April, when the seas are calmer and flights more reliable; during the summer monsoon, strong winds lash the island and make travel difficult. Life moves slowly here, and patience is essential.
t.sheikhali khan@32.9,51.4:
Out on the high, dry plain north-west of Isfahan, a village called Sheikhali Khan sits among fields, orchards and mud-brick walls, and it is the kind of place most travellers never stop in. That is exactly why it is interesting. This is qanat country. For about three thousand years, people on the Iranian plateau have tapped groundwater at the foot of the mountains with gently sloping tunnels dug by hand, bringing water by gravity for kilometres to villages and fields. From the air you can see the lines of shaft openings, like rows of craters, marching across the land. The Persian qanat is listed by UNESCO, and the Vazvan qanat, north of here, is one of the inscribed examples.

The landscape is stark and beautiful: bare brown mountains, pale earth, sudden patches of green wherever water arrives, poplars and walnut trees around the villages, and in spring the blossom of almond and apricot. The light is hard and clear, and the nights can be surprisingly cold even after a hot day. The Zayandeh Rud, the river that made Isfahan possible, rises in the Zagros to the west, though in recent years its flow through the city has often failed.

Isfahan itself, less than an hour away, is one of the great cities of the Islamic world, with Naqsh-e Jahan Square, the Shah and Sheikh Lotfollah mosques and the old bridges over the river. The town of Gaz to the north shares its name with Isfahan's famous sweet, a nougat made with pistachios and the sap of a tamarisk-like shrub, and you will find it sold everywhere in the region.

Riding in Iran is an adventure in the full sense. Rules on motorcycles have long been complicated, with restrictions on larger engines for local riders, while foreign riders usually come on their own bikes with the right temporary import papers; check the current situation well before you go, because it changes. Roads on the plateau are generally straight and fast, with good surfaces on main routes and erratic driving everywhere. Fuel is cheap and available in towns such as Najafabad and Khomeyni Shahr, both within half an hour, but stations can have queues. Carry plenty of water, dress modestly, and expect generous hospitality.
t.socotra h@12.3,53.6:
Socotra looks like the set of a science fiction film. Inland, the land rises to limestone plateaus such as Dixam, where the dragon's blood trees grow in the greatest numbers, cut by deep canyons with pools of water. The island's people speak Soqotri, a language related to the ancient languages of southern Arabia, and they live from fishing, goat herding and the date palms of the valleys.

Socotra has been extremely difficult to reach in recent years, with limited flights and the political situation in Yemen affecting access, and travel usually involves a local tour operator, who will provide vehicles and drivers. From June to September, the south-west monsoon brings very strong winds and rough seas, and much of the island is effectively closed to visitors.

Accommodation is mostly in simple camps on the beach or in the mountains. t.mahyar@32.3,51.8:
South of Isfahan, the road to Shiraz crosses a high, dry plain fringed with bare mountains, and caravans once crossed it in stages, resting each night in a caravanserai. At Mahyar, about forty kilometres from the city, one of these great roadside inns still stands: a square courtyard enclosed by brick walls, with arched rooms for travellers around it and stabling for animals behind, built in the Safavid period when Shah Abbas I made Isfahan his capital and encouraged trade along the roads. Many of Iran's caravanserais were listed together as a World Heritage Site in 2023 under the name Persian Caravanserai.

The plain here is high, over fifteen hundred metres, and the climate is dry, with hot summers and cold winters. In spring, the fields near villages turn green with wheat, and the mountains are capped with snow. The light is clear and sharp, and the colours of brick and earth glow in the evening.

The road from Isfahan to Shiraz is a busy highway, with heavy trucks and fast cars, and riding it is not a relaxing experience. Driving standards in Iran are challenging, and you need to be alert at all times. The minor roads into the villages and mountains are more interesting, but surfaces vary.

Travel to Iran is subject to complex political and practical considerations: many governments advise against travel, foreign bank cards do not work, and bringing a foreign motorcycle requires a carnet de passages. Check carefully before planning any trip. Fuel is cheap but rationed through fuel cards, and foreign travellers often need to buy fuel from station attendants at a higher price. Abrisham and Shahreza, on the road south, have services. Isfahan, with its great square and mosques, is one of the most beautiful cities in the world, and the obvious base for a visit.
t.qanat of zarch@31.9,54.4:
That is a qanat, and Zarch, east of Yazd, has one of the most famous in Iran, often described as among the longest in the world. Its main channel is dug by hand through the ground, with a line of vertical shafts every few dozen metres so that the diggers could haul up spoil and let in air. From the surface the shafts look like a row of craters running across the plain.

The qanat is the reason Yazd exists at all. The city lies on the edge of two great deserts, the Dasht-e Kavir and the Dasht-e Lut, and it gets almost no rain, yet it has grown for centuries on water that arrived through these tunnels. The old city is built of sun-dried mud brick, with wind towers rising from the roofs to catch and cool the air, and the old Zoroastrian community still lives here, keeping fire temples and the tradition of the Towers of Silence on the hills outside. In 2016 a group of eleven qanats, Zarch's neighbour among them, were listed together as a World Heritage property.

On a motorcycle this is desert riding of the classic kind. The highways around Yazd are broad, flat and straight, with long views, a hard sun and very little shade, and the hours between noon and four are better spent in a courtyard teahouse than on the asphalt. Spring and autumn are the good seasons; in midsummer the heat can be brutal, and winter nights are cold. Wind can pick up dust, so goggles or a closed visor are worth having. A short drive south-east the mud-brick village of Kharanaq, partly abandoned and partly restored, makes a good detour.

Yazd itself is a big, calm city, and it has fuel, food and a famous sweet shop tradition. Nothing at the qanat itself will serve you, so fill the tank and carry water before you go. Dress modestly and be ready for a conversation in broken English, because people here tend to be curious and generous with their time and their tea.
t.darsa@12.1,53.3:
Darsa is a speck of rock in the Indian Ocean, one of the small islands of the Socotra archipelago, which lies about two hundred and forty kilometres off the Horn of Africa and belongs politically to Yemen. It is the sort of place that makes sense only on a map: a low, dry island west of the main island of Socotra, with few or no permanent inhabitants, visited by fishermen and by seabirds. Together with its neighbour Samha and the big island, it forms one of the most remarkable natural treasures in the world, which UNESCO listed in 2008.

What is remarkable is the isolation. Socotra split from the African landmass millions of years ago and has been alone ever since, and about a third of its plant species are found nowhere else. The most famous is the dragon's blood tree, which looks like an upturned umbrella and weeps a deep red resin that was traded in antiquity as medicine and dye. The bottle trees, with swollen trunks and pink flowers, and the cucumber trees are just as strange. The surrounding sea has coral reefs, turtles and seabirds, and the place is often compared with the Galapagos.

There is no riding to be done on Darsa. The only way to reach it is by boat, and travel to the archipelago in general has been limited by the conflict in Yemen, with flights and shipping unreliable and the political situation changeable. On Socotra itself, there are a few paved roads and many dirt tracks, with strong winds, especially during the monsoon from June to September, when the sea is too rough for boats. The best time for visiting is from October to April, and local guides are essential.

t.mozd abad qanat@33.3,51.6:

t.bagh e pahlavanpur@31.6,54.4:

t.neyestanak@33.0,52.8:

The one associated with this area goes by the name Qanat of the Moon, and it belongs to the family of Persian qanats that UNESCO has recognised as a masterpiece of hydraulic engineering. t.qanat of the moon@33.4,52.4:

t.amin abad@31.7,52.1:

t.franz josef@-43.4,170.2:

t.st martins@45.4,-65.5:
St Martins is a small village on the Bay of Fundy coast of New Brunswick, and it lives by the tide. Twice a day the water retreats from the harbour and leaves the fishing boats resting on the mud, and twice a day it returns, rising several metres in a few hours. The Bay of Fundy has the highest tides in the world, and at St Martins the difference between low and high water is the height of a three-storey building. It is hard to understand until you have seen the same harbour at both extremes.

The village was a shipbuilding town in the nineteenth century, when the shore was lined with yards producing wooden square-riggers that sailed to Britain and beyond. The industry collapsed with the arrival of steel ships, and what remains are the captains' houses on the hillside, a lighthouse at Quaco Head and the quiet look of a place that was once richer. Two old covered bridges stand in the village, red-painted wooden structures that have crossed the creeks since the nineteenth century, and are favourite subjects for photographers.

The sea caves are the best-known attraction. At low tide, a stretch of beach below red sandstone cliffs opens up, and you can walk into caves worn into the rock, with high arched ceilings and floors of wet sand. The tide comes in quickly, so check the tide tables and keep an eye on the water. The red of the cliffs, the green of the spruce above and the brown of the mudflats make a strong contrast, and fog often drifts in from the sea, giving the coast a moody feel.

The road from Saint John, the nearest city, runs along Route 111 through forest and farmland, with tight bends and short climbs, before dropping into the village. The surface is generally fair, but frost heaves and patches appear in the spring. It is a quiet road for a motorcycle, and in good weather a joy. The Fundy Trail Parkway begins just beyond the village, offering a more scenic and elevated ride along the coast. Fog can arrive suddenly and temperatures drop, so carry a warm layer even in summer.

The village has a bakery, a couple of restaurants and a general store, and the seafood is excellent, with lobster rolls and haddock and chips being the staples. Fuel is limited, and the safest option is to fill the tank before heading out, either in Saint John or Sussex. Plan your visit around the tide, and bring a flashlight if you plan to explore the caves.
t.fundy trail parkway@45.4,-65.4:
The Fundy Trail Parkway is a short, slow, beautiful road along one of the wildest stretches of the Bay of Fundy, and it is built for looking rather than for speed. The parkway runs along the cliffs east of St Martins, through the Fundy Biosphere Reserve, with lookouts, short trails and a suspension bridge across the Big Salmon River, and the speed limit is low enough that you can take in the views without being hurried. It is a toll road, with an admission fee collected at the gate, and it is open seasonally, normally from spring to autumn.

The coast here is rugged, with steep forested slopes dropping to the sea, rocky headlands, and small beaches of pebbles and driftwood. At high tide, waves surge against the base of the cliffs, and at low tide the exposed seabed shows ribbons of seaweed and rock pools. The parkway is part of a long-term project to open a section of the coast that had no road, and the road was designed to blend into the landscape, with careful curves, stone guard walls and viewing platforms.

For motorcyclists, the ride is a pleasure in the way a gentle, scenic drive can be. The bends are smooth and well graded, the surface is excellent, and the gradients are steady, so you can enjoy the rhythm of the ride. In places the road climbs above the water, and the views stretch to the horizon. Take care in fog, which can come in without warning and reduce visibility to a few metres, and keep an eye out for wildlife, including moose, deer and bears, which sometimes cross the road. The suspension footbridge at the Big Salmon River is a good stop, where a walk across the gorge gives a view of the river meeting the sea.

The history of the coast is a story of logging, shipbuilding and isolated communities. In the nineteenth century, loggers floated timber down the rivers to sawmills at the coast, and the remains of old wharves and dams can still be seen in places. The tides here are among the highest in the world, and the water in the bay is cold, grey-green and always moving. Walkers can follow trails to quiet beaches, and in the autumn the forest above is a patchwork of red maple and yellow birch.

The nearest services are at St Martins, a short distance west, with Hampton and Sussex further inland, so fill the tank before you enter. A small interpretive centre and a cafe offer food and information, but the opening hours are seasonal. Allow at least two hours, and bring a layer for the sea breeze.
t.potrerillos@-32.9,-69.2:
Potrerillos is the point where the vineyards of Mendoza give way to the real mountains. The village sits beside a reservoir on the Mendoza River, about thirty-five kilometres from the city, and from here the road to Chile begins to climb. It is a green, irrigated place surrounded by dry brown hills, a contrast that makes the lake look very blue. In summer, locals come here to swim, sail and eat grilled meat, and the lakeside has an unpretentious holiday feel.

The road is Ruta 7, the old international route that links Mendoza with Santiago via the Paso de los Libertadores. It follows the river upstream in a canyon of tawny rock and tunnels, and it has been a major trade route since colonial times, when mule trains carried goods across the Andes. In the nineteenth century, General San Martín used a route in this region to lead his army across the mountains to liberate Chile, an epic undertaking that shaped South American history. The railway, now mostly abandoned, once ran here, and you can still see old bridges and stations along the valley.

For a rider, the road above Potrerillos is a real pleasure. The surface is generally good, the bends are wide and the scenery grows more dramatic with every kilometre. The air gets thinner, the colours more intense, and by the time you reach Uspallata you are in a high desert of reds, yellows and greys. Traffic includes heavy trucks heading for the border, so be careful on blind curves and when passing. The weather can change quickly, with wind and cold arriving fast above two thousand metres, and snow in winter can close the road.

Fuel is easiest in Mendoza before you leave, and again in the village of Uspallata farther along, so carry some margin. Mendoza itself has everything, including excellent wine, and many riders start here with a hearty breakfast of medialunas and coffee. Local specialities include grilled beef, empanadas and the famous Malbec, which is wonderful in the evening but not on the road.

Early morning is the best moment, with cool air and soft light on the rock. In summer, the heat in the lowlands builds quickly, and the mountains are the best escape.
t.puente del inca@-32.8,-69.9:
Puente del Inca is a natural stone bridge that has been coloured by a mineral spring. The bridge spans the Las Cuevas River in the high Andes, and the water, rich in sulphur and iron, has stained the rock in streaks of orange, yellow and rust. Hot springs rise beneath it, and the surface is coated with mineral crusts that look like paint. It sits at about 2,700 metres, in a valley of scree and bare mountains, with the white mass of Aconcagua, the highest peak in the Americas, somewhere beyond the ridges to the south.

Despite the name, the bridge was not built by the Inca. It formed naturally, as ice, sediment and mineral-rich water bonded together over thousands of years. The Inca did use trails in the region, but the colonial and later periods saw far more traffic, with mule caravans and travellers crossing on their way between Argentina and Chile. In the early twentieth century a hotel and thermal baths were built beside the bridge, and the ruins of that complex remain, a ghostly cluster of buildings half swallowed by the mineral deposits. Because of safety concerns, access to the bridge itself is limited, but you can see it from nearby viewpoints.

The road, Ruta 7, climbs to the site in broad bends along the valley, with a good surface and mountains closing in. The air is thin and cold, and the wind can be sharp. A line of small stalls sells souvenirs, mineral rocks and snacks, and a few simple cafes offer hot drinks and empanadas. The scenery is stark, and the colour of the rocks, red and ochre in the sun, is striking.

Uspallata, to the east, is the last reliable place to refuel on the Argentine side, and you should fill up before you start the climb, because the distances and altitudes ahead use more petrol than you might expect. The road beyond Puente del Inca leads to the Cristo Redentor tunnel and the old pass, and conditions depend heavily on the weather. In winter, snow and avalanche risk can close the road, sometimes for days.

Altitude can affect you, so take it easy and drink water. A short walk around the viewpoint is enough, and the late afternoon light makes the rocks glow.
t.molesworth cob cottage@-42.0,173.2:
Molesworth Station is the biggest farm in New Zealand, a vast stretch of high country in the north-east of the South Island covering over a hundred thousand hectares, and the cob cottage is one of its oldest buildings. It is a simple, thick-walled hut built of earth, in the style that early settlers brought from England, and it stands in a landscape of brown hills, braided rivers and enormous sky. The station is owned by the Crown and run as a working cattle farm, and it is managed with conservation in mind, so the grasslands, wetlands and wildlife are protected. The buildings are few and far between, and the sense of emptiness is overwhelming.

The road through the station, Molesworth Road, is a long, unsealed track of about 200 kilometres that links Hanmer Springs and the Awatere valley, and it has the reputation of being one of the great gravel roads in the country. It is open only in the warmer months, usually from late October to just before Easter, and it closes in winter when snow and floods make it impassable. The track passes through gates and across fords, and the gravel can be loose, corrugated and dusty, so a rider needs good tyres, a calm head and a lot of patience. There is a fee to use the road, and rules about not stopping to camp except in designated places, so check the current conditions before you go.

The cottage is a good place to stop and look around. It is built of cob, a mix of earth, straw and water, and has walls so thick that the rooms inside stay cool in summer and warm in winter. Beyond it, the valley opens into wide, tawny plains, with mountains rising on every side and herds of cattle moving slowly across the pasture. Hawks and falcons circle overhead, and in the evening the light turns the hills gold.

Blenheim, in the north, and Hanmer Springs, in the south, are the nearest places for fuel and supplies, and they are a long way from the middle of the track. Tell someone your plans, since mobile coverage is absent, and take a few spare hours, because it will take longer than you think.
t.acheron@-42.2,172.9:
Acheron is the southern gate of the Molesworth road, a spot where the pavement ends, the gravel begins and the high country starts, and a rider feels the change in the air. The Acheron River runs down from the mountains, clear and cold, and there is an old accommodation house nearby, a relic of the days when pack trains and drovers used this route to move stock and supplies across the hills. The landscape is broad and open, with tussock slopes, braided river beds and a sky that seems too big. Wind is common, and in the evening, the hills catch the last light in long gold streaks.

The Acheron is a place of preparation. Before you set off north across Molesworth, you check your tyres, your tank and your supplies, because there is no help for many kilometres. The gravel here is generally well graded, but it can be corrugated and loose, and heavy rain or snow melt can make fords and stream crossings tricky. In summer the air is dry and the dust is fine and pale, working into everything. Travel with a buff or scarf, and a spare tube.

The history of the region is a story of sheep and cattle. In the nineteenth century, big runs were set up in the high country, and sheep were driven over great distances to market. The land is hard and fragile, and the mountain slopes show scars of overgrazing from those days. The modern management of Molesworth is aimed at healing them, and there is a strong sense of landscape in recovery. Native birds, including falcons and pipits, are seen along the road, and the rivers hold trout.

The road is open seasonally, so check dates and conditions before heading out, and make sure you have a full tank. The nearest place for fuel is Hanmer Springs, a pleasant town about an hour's ride from here, famous for its hot pools, and it is also the place to buy food and supplies. If you want a comfortable night before the big ride, stay there and start early the next day. The view from the hills in the morning, with mist in the valleys and the sun rising over the ridges, is hard to beat.
t.castle hill@-43.2,171.7:
Castle Hill is a field of enormous limestone boulders scattered over a high basin in the Canterbury foothills, like the ruins of some giant's fortress, and it makes no sense until you stand among them. The rocks are weathered into towers, fins, arches and hollows, some of them many metres high, and the tussock between them is gold in summer and silver in frost. Māori called it Kura Tawhiti, meaning treasured place from a distant land, and it was used as a seasonal camp for people travelling to the West Coast in search of greenstone. The surrounding mountains, white with snow for much of the year, give the scene a stern, grand backdrop.

The boulders have become a world-famous place for climbing and bouldering, and on a good day you will see climbers working on the rock, chalk on their hands, pads on the ground. Others come just to wander, and the paths between the rocks are easy to follow. The scene was used in the Chronicles of Narnia film, as the site for a battle, and the connection has attracted fans. Do not climb on the rocks without proper skill, for the limestone is sharper than it looks. A short walk from the car park is enough for most, with signs explaining the geology and history.

State Highway 73, which runs past the site, is one of the great roads of the South Island, a scenic route between Christchurch and the West Coast, and here it crosses a high basin in long, open bends, with views of snowy ranges. The surface is good and the road is wide, with plenty of lay-bys. In winter, the road can be icy and snowy, and chains are sometimes required, so check conditions before you go. The wind blows hard across the basin, and the weather can change fast. Take warm clothing, even in summer.

Springfield, on the way up from Christchurch, has a few services, and Oxford is a bit farther back, so fill up before you climb. In Arthur's Pass, further west, supplies are limited. A flask of coffee and a sandwich are the best companions here, and a quiet half hour among the rocks at dawn or dusk is a real pleasure. Look out for kea, the mountain parrots, in the nearby hills.
t.arthurs pass@-42.9,171.6:
Arthur's Pass stands at 920 metres on the main divide of the Southern Alps, and its village is a small cluster of houses, a hotel, a visitor centre and a railway station, at the foot of a wall of rock, scree and snow. The pass was found in 1864 by the surveyor Arthur Dobson, and within a year a coach road had been built over it to carry gold miners to the West Coast. Before that Māori had used a route nearby. The railway followed, and an eight-and-a-half-kilometre tunnel under the range, finished in 1923, now carries the TranzAlpine train. The village exists because of these routes, and it is a base for walkers and climbers.

The mountains here are young, steep and rapidly eroding, and the landscape is raw: shingle fans, braided rivers, beech forest in the valleys and alpine meadows above. Weather comes in from the west with rain, cloud and wind, and the climate is wet and changeable. Snow can fall at any time of year, and the road has been closed many times by avalanches, floods and slips. A short walk from the village leads to the Devil's Punchbowl Falls, a waterfall of about 130 metres that thunders down a rock face into a deep pool. Wear waterproofs, as the spray is heavy.

The village is also home to the kea, the cheeky alpine parrots that are clever, curious and destructive. They will investigate anything, from a seat to a tyre, and will happily pull rubber from a bike. Do not leave anything loose on your machine, and do not feed them, however charming they look. They are protected and increasingly rare, but they have no respect for gloves.

The road, State Highway 73, is a classic, with sweeping views, long climbs and a good surface, and from Arthur's Pass it descends toward the west through Otira Gorge. Traffic is moderate, with trucks, campervans and tour coaches, and in winter the road may need chains. Fuel in the village is limited or unavailable, so fill up in Springfield on the east side or at Kumara or Hokitika to the west before you cross. There is a small shop and a café in the village, and a hot meal after a wet ride is welcome. Bring warm layers, because it can be cold.
t.otira gorge@-42.9,171.6:
The Otira Gorge is the steep western descent from Arthur's Pass, a short, dramatic drop where the road leaves the pass and plunges down a narrow, rocky valley with walls of broken stone on either side. The Otira River tumbles beside the road, cold, grey and loud. The cliffs are shaped by frost and rain, and rockfalls come down in storms. Waterfalls hang from the crags, and the bush grows dark and thick below. At the top of the gorge, the road crosses a long viaduct, built in 2017 to replace a section that kept slipping, and the structure is bold and modern against the wild background.

For a rider, the gorge is the real deal. The road falls steeply, with tight bends, a narrow carriageway and a heavy flow of trucks and tour coaches, and you need to concentrate. Use engine braking, keep to your side of the road and take the corners wide and slow. The surface can be wet or covered in debris, and the drop is a long one. In rain and cloud, visibility is poor, and the road can close for slips and snow, so check before you go. The ride up from the west is easier on the nerves, with a longer view and a satisfying climb.

At the foot of the gorge lies the village of Otira, a former railway town that once housed workers on the great tunnel, and now holds a handful of homes and a historic hotel. West Coast rain is legendary, and Otira receives huge amounts of it, with several metres a year. The result is lush, mossy rainforest and rivers that rise fast after storms. Sandflies are part of the picture, and you may be glad of repellent when you stop. The old coach road, a rough track, can be seen in places beside the new road.

Arthur's Pass village has limited services, and the real options are Springfield on the east or Kumara and Hokitika on the west, so start with a full tank. A short stop at a lookout near the top gives a fine view of the upper gorge and the viaduct. Wear waterproofs, and ride in the morning if you can, when traffic is lighter, and the weather is often clearer.
t.qasr e bahram@34.8,52.2:
No town is listed nearby, and that is the point: this is a country of long distances, of gravel plains, salt crusts and distant ranges, where a few hundred people live around a spring and a stand of poplars. Garmsar, on the northern side, is the nearest place with regular services that I can name with confidence.

Qasr means fortress or palace in Persian, and in a landscape like this the word usually points to a fortified building that served travellers, a caravanserai or a small stronghold set at a day's journey from the next one. For centuries the road along the edge of the Dasht-e Kavir, the Great Salt Desert, carried silk, spices and pilgrims, and the caravan stops were built of mud brick and baked clay, with thick walls, a single gate and rooms around a courtyard for animals and people.

Riding here is about heat and distance. In summer the temperature on the plain climbs well past forty degrees, the tarmac is soft in the afternoon and the wind carries fine dust, so start before dawn and rest in the middle of the day. Winters are cold, with frost at night. Spring is the kindest season, when the hills are briefly green and the wild tulips and poppies bloom on the slopes. Roads are generally straight and good along the main highway, but side tracks are sandy and unmarked.

Do not count on services off the main road. Carry water, fill the tank at every opportunity, and keep some food with you. Tea is the universal courtesy, and a driver or farmer who stops to talk will often offer a glass from a flask. Check current travel advice and permit conditions for Iran before planning, and make sure your papers and insurance are in order, as the rules for foreign motorcyclists are strict. Bring a map and a downloaded route, because the signal is unreliable.
t.izadkhast@31.5,52.1:
Īzadkhāst looks like a ship that ran aground in the desert. The old village sits on a narrow rocky outcrop, and its mud-brick houses climb the sides of the rock, with a deep gully on each flank. Its position, on the old caravan road between Isfahan and Shiraz, made it a natural halt, and the village is dominated by a historic caravanserai and fortress of the Safavid period, built of mud brick and clay, whose walls seem to grow out of the rock. A bridge links the old town with the newer streets across the gully.

The landscape is high and dry, with a plateau at over two thousand metres, so the air is thin and the nights are cold even when days are hot. The soil is pale, the hills are bare and the sky is huge. Winter brings frost and occasionally snow, while summer sun is fierce, and the best seasons are spring and early autumn, when the light is clear and the orchards are in leaf. Dust devils spin across the flat ground in the afternoon.

Riding on the old road is a pleasure. The surface is generally good, with long straight sections across the plateau and curves where the road follows the contours of the hills. There is not much traffic, though trucks use the main highway nearby. You may find stretches of gravel where the road is repaired, and the occasional flock of sheep, with a shepherd who waves.

No town is listed close to this spot, so plan fuel ahead. Fill up in a larger town before leaving the main road, carry water and expect basic services in the village. The ride pairs this place with Gaz, a town near Isfahan that gives its name to a famous nougat made with sap from the tamarisk tree, mixed with pistachios, almonds and sugar, and sold in every Iranian city. Buy a box as a gift, and try some with strong tea. As with all travel in Iran, check the current advice and your insurance in advance.
t.westport@-41.8,171.6:
Westport sits at the mouth of the Buller River on the north end of New Zealand's West Coast, a working town that grew up on coal and gold. The Māori knew the river as Kawatiri, and European settlers arrived in the 1860s when gold was found upstream, then stayed for the coal dug from the high plateau at Denniston, whose steep incline railway was one of the engineering marvels of its day. The coal trade still shapes the town, and the harbour and the long quay give it a plain, practical character that suits the coast.

Westport is also where the drama of the coast begins. To the west the road runs out to Cape Foulwind, a headland with a walkway and a New Zealand fur seal colony, and the name is a reminder of Captain Cook's bad weather in 1770. South of the town the highway squeezes between the Tasman Sea and the forested hills, passes the cliffs of the Paparoa range, and arrives at Punakaiki, where the Pancake Rocks, layered limestone stacks, blow spray through blowholes on a rising tide. From here the road continues toward Greymouth and the glaciers further south, about a hundred kilometres to the next big town.

The riding is superb but demanding. The highway has long coastal stretches with surf crashing on one side and rainforest on the other, interrupted by narrow one-lane bridges and tight bends, and the West Coast is one of the wettest parts of the country, so be ready for rain and slippery paint on the road. Sandflies at every stop are the other local feature, and a long-sleeved jacket and a bit of repellent help. On a clear day you can see the Southern Alps rise white in the distance.

Fuel and food are easy in Westport itself, and you should fill up properly before you leave because stations thin out on the road south. The coast road is quiet in winter, though cold and wet, and best from late spring to autumn. Order a plate of whitebait fritters if the season is right, as the Coast has a long tradition of them.
t.matapedia@48.0,-67.0:
Where the Matapédia river runs into the Restigouche, the Gaspé peninsula begins, and so does one of Canada's best salmon rivers. The village of Matapédia is a small place of a few hundred people squeezed between the water and forested Appalachian hills, right on the border between Quebec and New Brunswick, and for anyone riding Route 132 it is both a doorway and a full stop. The big loop around the Gaspésie, nearly nine hundred kilometres, is usually started here or finished here, and arriving after days of coast and cliff, you feel the road softening into river valley.

The river is the story. Atlantic salmon run up the Restigouche and Matapédia every summer, and fly fishermen have come for more than a century, sometimes staying in old fishing lodges beside the water. The Mi'gmaq people have fished and lived on these banks for much longer. Just downstream, at Pointe-à-la-Croix, a naval battle in 1760 sank the last French relief ships sent to Canada, and the little interpretation centre there tells the story of this forgotten final act of the Seven Years' War in North America.

The riding on the Matapédia valley road is gentle and elegant. Route 132 follows the water through spruce and maple, with long, easy sweeps and the occasional covered bridge or old railway station. Traffic is light, and the surface is generally good, though frost heaves can disturb it in spring. Moose are common, particularly at dusk, and a rider on a fast bike should be especially careful from dusk to dawn. In autumn, the maples turn scarlet and the whole valley burns with colour, which is the time most people recommend.

For fuel and food, the larger town is Campbellton, on the New Brunswick side, about twenty kilometres away, with supermarkets, restaurants and several filling stations. Matapédia itself has a couple of simple places to eat, and the local speciality is salmon, smoked or grilled. Cash and card are both accepted, but small places can be limited.

The border between provinces is open, but a time zone shift can catch you out, as New Brunswick keeps Atlantic time while this part of Quebec uses Eastern. Summers are warm, winters long and snowy, and the road is best from June to October.
t.nelson@-41.3,173.3:
Nelson claims to be one of the sunniest places in New Zealand, and the locals say it with the smugness of people who have earned it. The city sits at the top of the South Island on Tasman Bay, with a wide sheltered beach, a backdrop of hills and the mountains of Kahurangi and Abel Tasman beyond. About fifty-nine thousand people live here, and it has a reputation for craft beer, pottery, galleries and a general willingness to take life slowly.

The city was founded in 1841 by the New Zealand Company, and a hilltop monument marks the supposed geographical centre of the country, reached by a short walk up Botanical Hill. Long before the settlers came, Māori had lived along the bay, and the sheltered coastline and fertile land were prized. Today the area is a centre for hops, apples, kiwifruit and seafood, and the nearby Mapua wharf has smoked fish and ice cream.

For riders, Nelson is the gateway to two excellent roads. Eastward, State Highway 6 climbs over the Rai Saddle and runs through forest to Pelorus Bridge and Havelock, the green-lipped mussel capital, from where the winding Queen Charlotte Drive, with the sounds spread below, leads to Picton. Westward and north, State Highway 60 climbs Takaka Hill to roughly 800 metres on a series of hairpins, through limestone and marble country dotted with caves and sinkholes, and drops into Golden Bay, where beaches are wide and quiet. Both roads are twisty and scenic, and both can be foggy or wet. Slips and roadworks sometimes close sections after heavy rain, so check before committing, and be careful of gravel on corners and logging trucks.

Practically, Nelson has everything. Fuel is plentiful in town and in nearby Richmond, with more than fourteen thousand people, and the cafes of the city centre are a good place for a long breakfast before a big day. Fuel on the Takaka Hill route is limited, so fill before leaving. The best seasons are late spring and early autumn, when the days are clear and warm, and the summer crowds are thin.
t.ancient garden of pasargadae@30.2,53.2:
Pasargadae was the first capital of the Persian Empire, built by Cyrus the Great in the middle of the sixth century BC, after he defeated the Medes and the Lydians and made himself master of most of the known world. It stands on a high, open plain in Fars province, at about 1,900 metres, and what survives is spread out across the grassland: the tomb of Cyrus, a gabled stone chamber on a stepped platform; the stone bases of audience halls; a gatehouse with a carved winged figure; and the lines of a garden, the earliest known example of the symmetrical Persian chahar bagh, divided by water channels into four parts.

The tomb is the sight. Made of pale limestone blocks, it rises in six steps to a small room with a gabled roof, simple and austere, and the ancient writers described how Alexander visited and was moved to find that the great king lay in so modest a tomb. The inscription the Greek writers quoted is long gone, but the tomb stands, and the sense of space around it is extraordinary. The British Museum holds the Cyrus Cylinder, a clay record of his policies, found in Babylon, and it is often cited as an early statement of tolerance, though historians debate how to read it.

The riding is easy and open. The road from Shiraz runs north-east for about 130 kilometres across a high plateau, passing Persepolis and the Marvdasht plain, then climbing gently to the site. The surface is good, with long straight stretches and a few bends, and the air is clear and thin. Winters can be cold, with frost and snow, and summers hot and dry, so spring and autumn are best. In April the surrounding fields are green and dotted with poppies.

Pasargad is a town of about thirty thousand people, immediately next to the site, so fuel, food and lodging are no problem. A few small restaurants serve grilled chicken, rice and yoghurt, and you can buy bread and fruit at local shops. Arrive early to avoid the heat and tour buses, and walk the full site, since there is almost no shade. Take water and a hat, and give yourself time to sit by the tomb and let the wind do its work.
t.shiryaevo@53.4,50.0:
Shiryaevo lies in the Samara Bend, the great loop of the Volga where the river swings around the Zhiguli Mountains. The hills here are not high, topping out near three hundred and seventy meters, but they rise suddenly from the water in forested cliffs and ravines, and in a country of flat plains they make a spectacular sight. Limestone and dolomite form the rock, and the slopes carry oak, linden and maple, with steppe plants on the south-facing ridges. The Zhiguli Nature Reserve protects part of the range and some rare plants that survived the Ice Age here.

The village is best known for a painter. In the summer of 1870, the young Ilya Repin came to Shiryaevo with fellow students to sketch the Volga, and the sketches he made of barge haulers became the basis for his famous painting Barge Haulers on the Volga. A small museum in the village commemorates his stay and displays his drawings, and the quiet streets above the river give a sense of what the countryside looked like then. The hills are also rich in legend. The folk hero and rebel Stenka Razin is said to have hidden here with his band of river pirates in the seventeenth century, and many caves and cliffs carry his name.

The riding is a high point of the Volga region. The road along the river follows the shore in gentle bends, with views of the water, the hills and passing ships, and climbs into the wooded slopes in places. The surface is variable, with good stretches and patches of broken asphalt, and traffic is lively on summer weekends when people from Samara and Tolyatti come to swim and picnic. Early morning is the best time, with mist on the water and few other travelers. The weather can be hot in July and August, and thunderstorms build quickly in the afternoon.
